Christopher Kelly, aged 40, killed 51-year-old Dorothy Beattie by strangulation at her Dunoon residence in Argyll and Bute on May 22nd. The High Court in Glasgow heard that the fatal attack was triggered by an insult Ms. Beattie allegedly made about Kelly's children. Kelly, who had confessed to a doctor, resulting in his apprehension, pleaded guilty to culpable homicide, a lesser charge than the original murder charge. The court learned that Kelly, previously Ms. Beattie’s support worker due to her health problems, including seizures, had formed a bond with the divorced woman, and they often socialized. The strangulation happened at her home following the reported "derogatory" remarks about his children; he strangled her, departed, and later returned to find her dead.

State Prosecutor Marilyn Mosby announced revised charges in the Freddie Gray case on Thursday, standing by the second-degree murder charge. Gray's death, which followed a week after he suffered a severe spinal injury while in police custody in April, sparked extensive protests that devolved into riots and looting in Baltimore. Mosby stated that altering charges during an ongoing investigation is a standard and suitable procedure as new evidence emerges. Although the grand jury declined to indict on the false imprisonment charges initially brought by Mosby, who claimed Gray's arrest was illegal, they added new reckless endangerment charges not present in the initial announcement three weeks earlier. Mosby insists that Gray's neck was broken while he was handcuffed and inside a police van, and that officers ignored his repeated pleas for medical assistance.

The family of Baboucarr Ceesay, a 21-year-old Gambian, is mourning his likely death in a recent Libyan shipwreck. His aunt, Jessica Sey from Cheltenham, voiced the family's sorrow, highlighting the importance of accountability and greater understanding of the dangers migrants face. She insisted that those profiting from migrant exploitation "have got to be held to account." Mrs. Sey also underscored the local impact of this global issue, describing her nephew's fatal attempt to reach the UK as "a desperate way out." Although a gifted footballer with a bright future in Gambia, his desire for a better life in Europe led him and a friend to travel by boat from Banjul to Guinea before undertaking a hazardous journey across the Sahara.

For two years running, an AI algorithm has proven more accurate than BBC pundit Mark Lawrenson in predicting football results, leading its developers to invite fantasy football players to compete against it. The researchers believe the algorithm can help players build winning fantasy teams. Fantasy football, created in 1971 by Bernie Donnelly, allows participants to form virtual teams using real footballers and score points based on their real-world performances. This formerly niche hobby has grown into a large online business, featuring ad-supported websites, mobile apps, and betting options. Now, in the free Fantasy Premier League salary cap game, managers can assess their skills against Squadguru's AI in the "Challenge the Squadguru" league.

Reports indicate that the explosion took place at a camp providing food to displaced people who had escaped conflict in tribal areas near the Afghan border, a region reportedly used as a haven by Taliban and al-Qaeda militants. Police suspect the camp may also be providing shelter to militants. Although concerns have long existed regarding militant infiltration in Jalozai and other similar camps, no group has claimed responsibility for the attack, which is atypical for Pakistani refugee camps. According to BBC's M Ilyas Khan in Islamabad, recent arrests by a government-backed tribal force of individuals linked to the Lashkar-e-Islam militant group have led police to suspect the bombing was an act of revenge. Live footage showed ambulances taking victims to hospitals while police investigated the bomb crater amidst the wreckage.

A city council report on the July 2015 yacht races highlighted both positive and negative outcomes. The event, organized by TeamOrigin Events as the debut of the sailing series and the launch of Sir Ben Ainslie Racing's (BAR) campaign for the 35th America's Cup, boosted tourism and enhanced the city's reputation. However, it also exposed problems, including unclear ticketing procedures for spectators and unattractive barriers. A key change for future races will be the elimination of evening entertainment. While Saturday's races attracted approximately 100,000 spectators, Sunday's races were canceled due to inclement weather, resulting in the shutdown of public viewing areas and disappointing attendees like the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. Furthermore, social media users expressed dissatisfaction with the standard of spectator facilities.

Security forces used tear gas and live rounds to break up a largely Shia Muslim protest in Baghdad against government corruption and poor security, leading to at least 50 protester injuries. While an initial curfew has been lifted, this is the second time this month demonstrators have entered the city's government zone. Shia cleric Moqtada Sadr condemned the violent crackdown, supporting the protesters' "peaceful [and] spontaneous revolt." The protesters argue that the government is failing to implement critical reforms as it fights the Islamic State group (IS) and deals with declining oil revenues. The Sunni jihadist group, which still controls territory in western and northern Iraq and has claimed responsibility for several recent deadly attacks, is a major concern. Some protesters managed to enter the prime minister's office and the parliament building, both located within Baghdad's Green Zone, which also houses important government buildings and numerous foreign embassies.

Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister Peter O'Neill announced a mutual agreement with Australian Immigration Minister Peter Dutton in Port Moresby to close the Manus Island Regional Processing Centre. This decision was prompted by the PNG Supreme Court's April decision declaring the detention of asylum seekers and refugees there unconstitutional. Although the immediate closure of the center, which houses 854 men, is not planned, O'Neill stated that different strategies are being investigated and implemented. He stressed the importance of a careful, well-considered plan that takes into account the needs of Papua New Guineans alongside the well-being of the asylum seekers and refugees, within the framework of Australia's policy of offshore processing for boat arrivals.

BBC Three's online platform is set to deliver weekly coverage of the Gfinity Elite Series, a competition featuring 160 gamers vying for a £225,000 prize pool before a live audience. Despite e-sports' established online presence, an expert suggests the BBC's participation has the potential to attract a broader audience. The agreement encompasses exclusive content broadcasts from the Gfinity tournament in west London, focusing on gamers battling it out in Street Fighter V, Counter Strike: Global Offensive, and Rocket League. Although platforms like Twitch and YouTube are the primary e-sports streaming destinations, traditional television channels, such as Ginx in the UK, also broadcast events. IHS analyst Piers Harding-Rolls notes that the BBC asserts its Gfinity coverage will be "on a much larger scale" compared to its prior e-sports highlight programs.

This interactive display can simulate a smartphone's touchscreen, a full computer keyboard, or piano keys. Additionally, the laser projector can project images and videos onto walls. Unveiled at Lenovo's Tech World in Beijing were the Smart Cast phone and a new smartwatch. Lenovo claims its compact 34mm x 26mm x 5mm laser projector removes the need for manual focusing, ensuring sharp images on walls or any flat surface. A demo video shows that rotating the lens mount changes the device from standard wall projection to "surface mode," facilitating projection onto surfaces.

Amid persistent terrorism concerns, a Metropolitan Police Federation survey gauging officer opinions on firearms showed that only 6% of the 11,000 participants believed the existing number of armed officers was sufficient, even with the Met's intention to recruit an additional 600. Given the UK's "severe" international terrorism threat level since August 2014, the poll highlighted that 43% desired more specialist firearms officers, 26% supported routinely arming all officers, and 12% would refuse to carry a firearm. The data also showed 2,139 authorized firearms officers (6.7% of the overall force), 3,974 firearms operations from March 2015 to March 2016, and 7 cases of police firearm discharge in 2015-16. Strong backing for Tasers was apparent, with 75% favoring universal availability. The survey also investigated whether the presence of armed police provided reassurance.

Geraint Thomas, at 28, is crucial to Team Sky's strategy to help Chris Froome win his second Tour de France in a row. Thomas voiced worries about the dangerous cobblestone paths, particularly given Froome's X-ray after a stage four crash. He stressed that rain could quickly ruin a rider's chances after a year's preparation. Thomas hopes for dry weather to reduce the chance of crashes. Froome, 29, crashed early in the 163.5km stage four when his wheel touched another rider in the pack. Despite a scraped hip and wrist, he was treated and kept racing. Marcel Kittel won the stage, and Froome is now seventh overall, only two seconds behind leader Vincenzo Nibali.

By the end of June, the Supreme Court is expected to rule on a Virginia school district's right to prevent a transgender student, who was assigned female at birth, from using the boys' restroom. The possibility of a 4-4 tie exists due to the vacancy left by Antonin Scalia's death. This case underscores the national divide among school districts regarding transgender bathroom policies, frequently tied to birth certificates. Gloucester County, Virginia, appealed to the Supreme Court, resulting in a temporary suspension of a lower court's decision that allowed transgender student Gavin Grimm to use the male restrooms. Grimm, who identifies as male, filed a lawsuit against the school board after publicly revealing his transgender status during his freshman year.

Angus Campbell, head of Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, criticized the unfair airfares, noting that the airline serving Stornoway provided cheaper flights to destinations like the Algarve. A Facebook campaign protesting this disparity has attracted significant support, with over 11,000 "likes." Loganair, Flybe's partner for island routes, justified its pricing structure by mentioning discounted fares for specific groups, including children, students, medical patients, and island residents. Campbell stressed that lowering air travel expenses is a primary goal of Our Islands Our Future, an initiative focused on achieving greater self-governance for the Shetland, Orkney, and Western Isles councils. He underscored the problem of expensive flights, using a £351 round-trip fare from Stornoway to Glasgow on Flybe as an illustration, and observing that similar flights in other regions were less costly.

In 2012, the Northern Echo reported that Cleveland Police allegedly tried to monitor the communications of six individuals—including its journalists, a staff member, and a lawyer—after the paper published a front-page article. The Police Federation lodged a formal complaint with the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC), while the police force declined to comment to the BBC. The Echo alleges that police used the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA), meant for crime prevention or public safety surveillance, to identify the source of information for a story revealing institutional racism within the police, based on an internal police document. A Cleveland Police spokesperson told the paper that she could "neither confirm nor deny" the use of a RIPA application to track the phone activity of three journalists, a police officer, a solicitor, and the former chairman of the Cleveland Police Federation.

Research on employees and managers showed that a quarter of new fathers took no paternity leave, while fewer than 10% took more than the statutory two-week minimum. The Institute of Leadership & Management (ILM), who carried out the study, blamed this on ingrained employer prejudice and financial worries experienced by new fathers. The ILM's results indicate that the shared parental leave scheme, launched by the government in April 2015, is unlikely to succeed unless employer biases are tackled. ILM chief executive Charles Elvin stressed the importance of shared parental leave for women's career progression, but the study reveals cultural barriers preventing fathers from taking both the required and extra leave, underscoring an enduring "cultural expectation" that childcare is primarily the mother's responsibility.

On March 14th, Irish Coastguard Rescue Helicopter 116 crashed with a crew of four. Captain Dara Fitzpatrick was recovered from the water but did not survive. The search continues for the remaining crew, with divers resuming operations on Friday, aided by improved weather. Garda Superintendent Tony Healy confirmed the divers are "actively working" on the seabed, prioritizing the crew's recovery and ceasing operations at nightfall. Jurgen Whyte, chief inspector of the IAAIU, reported the data recorder's retrieval from the seabed near Blackrock at 4:30 PM, with plans to transport it to Dublin before forwarding it to the UK's air accident investigation branch for analysis.

The "Vermeer's Women: Secrets and Silence" exhibition has been a resounding success, drawing over 130,000 attendees since its October debut. A primary highlight is Vermeer's small yet impactful "The Lacemaker," on loan from The Louvre and making its UK debut. In response to the exhibition's immense popularity, the museum will extend its hours for the final two weeks. Curator Betsy Wiseman credits much of the exhibition's triumph to "The Lacemaker," emphasizing its exceptional rarity as a loan from The Louvre, where it is treasured almost as much as the Mona Lisa. Additional noteworthy pieces featured include "A Lady At The Virginals With A Gentleman (The Music Lesson)" from The Royal Collection and "A Young Woman Seated At A Virginal" from London's National Gallery.

In July 2016, the remains of Helen Bailey, 51, were found in a cesspool at her Royston, Hertfordshire home, several months after she disappeared on April 11th. Her fiance, Ian Stewart, is on trial for her murder and denies the charges. At St Albans Crown Court, Edward Farmer, a witness, initially claimed to have seen Bailey alone in a dark Range Rover or similar 4x4 on Charlotte Street, near her holiday home in Broadstairs, Kent, sometime between mid-April and June. He later admitted the sighting could have occurred earlier. This testimony potentially weakened the defense's claim that two menacing men abducted Bailey and took her to Broadstairs. When questioned about the date, Farmer approximated the sighting to be "five, maybe six weeks" prior to his police interview.

Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting indicated that policymakers were worried about stock market instability and global economic fragility. However, they were reluctant to express these concerns openly, concerned about potential miscommunication. Officials emphasized the fundamental resilience of the US economy, citing it as a key factor in their decision to halt quantitative easing (QE), a bond-buying program designed to keep long-term interest rates low and encourage spending. The meeting summary indicated a general consensus that the economy was robust enough to continue moving towards full employment, justifying the conclusion of the QE program. US markets reacted calmly to the news, with the Dow Jones briefly rising before falling back.

Robin Waistell blamed the unsaleability of his Maesteg property on the rail authority's neglect in managing a large knotweed infestation on the adjacent embankment. This case was viewed as potentially precedent-setting for homeowners whose properties are impacted by knotweed originating from railway land. Network Rail acknowledged that they would carefully review the court's ruling, although their request for an immediate appeal was rejected. After losing the Cardiff case to Waistell and his neighbor, Network Rail anticipates incurring substantial legal costs. Waistell, a 70-year-old widower, had moved to the bungalow from Spain after his wife's passing, intending to eventually move back, but the knotweed's spread from Network Rail's land prevented him from selling the property.

Rex Tillerson's confirmation hearing included statements that could damage relations with Beijing, especially regarding China's creation of artificial islands on contested reefs in the South China Sea, an area with competing territorial claims. Recent evaluations indicate potential military installations on some of these islands. Speaking to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Tillerson likened China's island construction to Russia's annexation of Crimea. He argued that the US should strongly insist that China cease island construction and block access to them. China's island-building has intensified regional tensions, as Beijing claims sovereignty over nearly all of the South China Sea, a claim that conflicts with those of Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, Malaysia, and Brunei. Despite an international court ruling in July against China's claims, prompted by a case filed by the Philippines, Beijing has dismissed the decision.

Aberdeen City Council is considering issuing index-linked bonds, contingent on positive market conditions. As the first Scottish council to earn a credit rating (Aa2 from Moody's), Aberdeen intends to use the bond proceeds to finance its £1 billion capital investment program. Council leader Jennifer Laing described the potential bond issuance as a significant milestone for the city, marking another first for a Scottish local authority after receiving its credit rating. She highlighted that this forward-thinking method of capital funding illustrates their dedication to protecting the revenue budget, which is vital for providing key public services.

In Chicago, Gwen Jorgensen of the United States took first place, with Stanford finishing second and Holland third. Jorgensen's strong running performance clinched her win, marking her 15th consecutive victory and securing her second straight world championship. Stanford, representing Wales and a former world champion, acknowledged the difficulty of the demanding qualification process. Holland was delighted to finish on the podium, particularly after breaking away with only two other athletes. Jorgensen's total time for the 1.5km swim, 40km bike ride, and 10km run was 1:55:36, while Stanford, the second Welsh woman after Hannah Mills to qualify for Rio, trailed by 29 seconds.

GMB Scotland is considering a strike among its offshore employees, following Unite's similar action, due to concerns about job security. Union officials will seek approval from the regional committee to hold a strike vote for members under the Offshore Contractors Agreement. This action is in response to planned job losses and wage cuts by North Sea oil and gas firms, citing persistently low oil prices. The decision comes after unsuccessful talks on Friday between the two unions, and the Offshore Contractors Association (OCA), representing offshore contractors. The Offshore Contractors Agreement covers workers in mechanical, electrical, construction, maintenance, design, project engineering, fabrication, decommissioning, and related fields. GMB Scotland's regional officer, John Kelly, criticized certain oil companies and contractors for what he called "blatant opportunism" in their attempts to severely worsen workforce terms and conditions.

In the first half, Walsall's attack was sharper, but Albion's Jon McLaughlin blocked shots from Paul Downing and Romaine Sawyers. Burton's Stuart Beavon entered Walsall's penalty area but couldn't score. Wigan's win against Bury means Albion's lead at the top of the league is now just two points, with Walsall staying fourth. Burton Albion's Nigel Clough told BBC Radio Derby the game was "no classic," a tight affair with few opportunities, but valued the clean sheet and point. He conceded their passing was better in their previous game but praised the team's improved toughness and defense. Walsall's head coach, Sean O'Driscoll, stated.

In his White House talks with President Obama, the Prime Minister raised issues surrounding extradition treaties. Critics argue the existing agreement is skewed towards the US, suggesting it demands less evidence for extraditing UK citizens. Yet, a senior judge reviewing the treaty in 2011 found it fair to Britons. The BBC's Nick Robinson noted Mr. Cameron discussed the real-world effects of these rules during Wednesday's two-hour meeting. The Prime Minister's three-day US visit occurs amidst ongoing debate over the 2003 US-UK extradition treaty, fueled by high-profile cases like Christopher Tappin and Gary McKinnon. Groups such as Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights have urged the government to renegotiate the treaty, citing its perceived imbalance.

Fiscal Kombat casts players as Mr. Melenchon, who battles oligarchs and political adversaries across urban landscapes. The objective is to transfer riches from the wealthy elite to support Melenchon's political platform. Players must accumulate the largest possible amount of funds while evading deadly assaults from affluent figures. Melenchon faces off against a roster of "boss" characters, such as former President Nicolas Sarkozy, IMF head Christine Lagarde, tax dodger Jerome Cahuzac, and L'Oreal magnate Liliane Bettencourt. He also clashes with Emmanuel Macron and Francois Fillon, presidential contenders in the 2017 French election. According to Le Monde, the game was conceived by Melenchon's followers on the Jeuxvideo.com forum and enjoys his complete endorsement.

The merger of Bouygues Telecom and Vivendi's SFR is intended to create France's top mobile operator, consolidating the market to three major players. Altice, Numericable's owner, has also made a confidential offer for SFR. If the proposed Bouygues Telecom and SFR union, combining the second and third largest mobile providers, is approved, it would overtake Orange as the market leader. This merger requires approval from French and EU regulators due to competition concerns, mirroring similar issues with Telefonica's attempt to acquire E-Plus in Germany. Analysts view the Bouygues proposal as a sign of increasing consolidation within the mobile sector.

Doreen Collyer, a 60-year-old retired University of Chester lecturer, tragically died in a shark attack during a scuba diving excursion in Perth on Sunday. Authorities suspect a 16-foot great white shark was the culprit, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC). Her husband, David Collyer, remembered her as his "loving wife" and a "beautiful person." The couple had moved to Australia from Neston, Cheshire, about five years ago. Mrs. Collyer held an advanced open water diving certification. ABC reported that her diving companion brought her to the shore, but she died from her injuries. Prof Annette McIntosh-Scott from the University of Chester expressed her sorrow, recalling Mrs. Collyer as a "hugely valued and loved member of staff" who dedicated 15 years to the Faculty of Health and Social Care, leaving a lasting impression on teaching, child healthcare, and student support.

A U.S. warbler, probably detoured by Hurricane Gert while migrating through South America, has been seen in England, a landmark event confirmed by Martin Cade of the Portland Bird Observatory, who described the find as "pretty amazing." Typically found in the United States, these birds regularly migrate between North and South America. Cade suspects the hurricane's winds transported the warbler across the Atlantic from the Caribbean, mirroring a recent warbler sighting at Mizen Head in southwest Ireland. The robin-sized bird seems "active and feeding well," possibly preparing for a southward migration toward Spain and Africa, Cade suggests. The unusual sighting, announced on Monday, drew birdwatchers from far-flung areas, including the Midlands, South Wales, and Yorkshire.

Despite Alexis Sanchez having only a year remaining on his contract, Arsene Wenger is confident that the Chilean forward, instrumental in Arsenal's FA Cup semi-final win against Manchester City, will sign a new agreement and stay with the Gunners. The Arsenal manager affirmed he would not sell the 28-year-old to a rival Premier League club. Amidst speculation about Wenger's own future – his contract expiring this season with a two-year extension proposed – the 67-year-old maintains he is already strategizing for next season's transfer targets, highlighting their significance to the club's long-term prospects.

Following Richard Matt and David Sweat's escape from Clinton Correctional Facility using power tools, Gene Palmer was apprehended and charged with promoting prison contraband, tampering with evidence, and official misconduct. This made him the second prison staff member arrested after Joyce Mitchell, who is already facing accusations of aiding the escape. Palmer was arraigned and subsequently released on bail. His lawyer, Andrew Brockway, admitted that Palmer had delivered the meat package but asserted that he was ignorant of the tools hidden inside and the inmates' escape plot. Brockway stated that Palmer is remorseful for his involvement and plans to enter a not-guilty plea. Clinton County District Attorney Andrew Wylie pointed out that Mitchell placed.

The H3 project, designed to consolidate administrative tasks across Hampshire and Oxfordshire's police, fire, and council services, targeted £5 million in yearly savings. Yet, since its launch in 2014, the Police Federation has documented numerous errors, particularly regarding payroll. Despite continued investment, Hampshire's Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) expects enhancements by May. A report for PCC Michael Lane revealed that H3 has complicated recruitment, made employee sick leave management more difficult, and increased officers' administrative workload, reducing their effectiveness. In February 2016, 1,300 officers faced pay errors, with incorrect allowance calculations following in March. Moreover, a 2015 BBC investigation found that payment delays to Hampshire County Council vendors had tripled under the new system. Law enforcement officials apprehended a 22-year-old Sleaford resident and a 25-year-old Bracknell resident on Thursday, suspecting them of involvement in several attempts to infiltrate Microsoft's networks between January and March. The arrests, made under the Computer Misuse Act—legislation against unauthorized computer access—followed allegations that the pair belonged to a wider collective plotting a cyberattack to pilfer Microsoft customer data. Det Sgt Rob Bryant stated that the South East Regional Organised Crime Unit (Serocu) conducted the raids and seized equipment believed to be connected to the alleged offenses.

Twenty-year-old Ariya Jutanugarn played a perfect round with six birdies, putting her in contention to surpass the tournament's record of 19-under-par. Mirim Lee of South Korea, who previously led, fell to second place after shooting a 69. Catriona Matthew of Scotland is currently in fourth, trailing by six strokes. Jutanugarn is seeking to become the first Thai golfer to secure a major victory, leveraging lessons learned from her near-win at the ANA Inspiration. Jutanugarn demonstrated remarkable composure in her third round, telling BBC Sport that she now understands how to handle pressure and is concentrating on the elements within her control.

At an IMF gathering in Washington, Christine Lagarde lauded the UK's economic approach as successful. She minimized differences between the IMF's deficit projections and the more optimistic figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility, attributing them to differing methodologies while asserting their fundamental agreement. Standing alongside George Osborne and Wolfgang Schaeuble, Lagarde pointed out that deficit forecasts are typically conservative in election years, reflecting uncertainty about the full implementation of planned policies. She also recognized the UK's achievement in combining spending reductions with revenue growth and highlighted the UK's relatively strong economic expansion in comparison to other European nations.

In response to the rapid growth and technological advancements within the private hire sector, Transport for London (TfL) is evaluating revised regulations for these companies. The proposed rules include mandatory English proficiency and route-finding assessments, the maintenance of a fixed office telephone line, and enabling customers to schedule rides up to a week ahead of time. Uber has voiced opposition, asserting that the changes would drastically change its operational model. Black cab drivers, who recently protested at City Hall, have been pushing for tighter controls. Uber's app, which uses GPS to connect riders with drivers, calculate fares, and handle electronic payments, offers a cheaper alternative to traditional taxis. TfL insists the consultation seeks to raise industry benchmarks, but Uber contends it is being unfairly targeted and that the suggested regulations would result in higher prices for consumers and increased traffic.

Music festival "superfans," predominantly male, are a major economic force, spending an average of £581 per year and often opting for VIP experiences or upgraded camping options. Distinguishing themselves from regular attendees, these dedicated enthusiasts are more inclined to purchase music in both physical and digital forms. An Eventbrite survey of 504 UK festival-goers reveals that these "superfans" wield considerable influence, shaping festival trends through their input. Comprising 28% of the festival audience, with 54% happy to attend alone, their allegiance is not guaranteed, as almost half (46%) believe festivals are becoming overly commercialized. The UK's vibrant music festival scene features over 100 annual events, from large-scale affairs like Glastonbury and T In The Park to more intimate and exclusive gatherings.

The pound surged, gaining 1.86% against the dollar to $1.32.40 and 1.73% against the euro to trade at €1.19.57. While the FTSE 100 briefly hit an 11-month peak, it subsequently fell back to close virtually flat at 6,680.69, down a slight 2.17 points or 0.03%. Conversely, the more domestically focused FTSE 250 rose by 68.75 points, a 0.4% increase, to reach 16,775.14. The property market, previously hit by Brexit concerns, was boosted by Galliford Try's forecast of meeting full-year profit expectations, sending its stock price up by 8.5%. Financial stocks, also impacted by the referendum's outcome, rebounded somewhat, with Aviva shares rising by 4.26% and Lloyds Banking Group also recording gains.

A fishing boat suffered significant damage in April after a submarine snagged its nets, pulling it 18 miles from the County Down shoreline. The skipper, while relieved his crew was unharmed, anticipated repair costs of approximately £10,000. Departing from standard procedure, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has now admitted a British submarine was responsible. The Royal Navy confirmed that "new information" confirmed a UK submarine damaged the MV Karen. Armed Forces Minister Penny Mordaunt addressed Parliament, offering sincere apologies for "the incident, the delay in identifying and addressing the events on that day, and their consequences," explaining that the submarine had mistakenly identified the Karen as a fishing vessel actively fishing.

The killing of Kian Delos Santos by police officers ignited public anger due to their claim that he was a drug peddler who fought back during arrest. However, CCTV footage appeared to contradict this, showing him being taken into custody by officers in civilian clothing. Accounts suggested he was on his knees when he was shot. His funeral in Manila was attended by hundreds, with some using the occasion to protest President Duterte's widely supported yet contentious anti-drug initiative. Reuters documented a procession of nuns, priests, and children marching from a church to the cemetery, chanting "justice for Kian, justice for all." During the funeral Mass, Kian's father, Saldy, passionately defended his son's innocence, condemned the police's behavior, and emotionally challenged their humanity, urging them to find comfort in the church.

Completed in less than a year, the new 72-kilometer channel runs alongside a portion of the original Suez Canal, facilitating simultaneous two-way traffic and accommodating larger vessels. On Saturday, a successful trial involved a convoy of international container ships navigating the channel, escorted by naval vessels and helicopters. The Sinai Peninsula, adjacent to the canal, has been plagued by persistent violence from Islamic militants, causing hundreds of fatalities since President Mohammed Morsi's removal in 2013. Nearly 150 years ago, the original Suez Canal, linking the Mediterranean and Red Seas, was opened. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi anticipates that this expanded canal, which presently handles 7% of global maritime commerce, will boost the nation's economy and generate employment opportunities.

James Carragher, previously imprisoned in 1993 and 2004 for sex crimes, receiving sentences of seven and fourteen years respectively, is now facing trial at Leeds Crown Court on 50 counts of indecent assault. These alleged crimes are said to have taken place between the 1970s and 1990s at St William's, a former Catholic-run home in Market Weighton, East Riding of Yorkshire, for boys with behavioral problems operated by the De La Salle order. Two other former employees of the institution have also been tried. Carragher, who managed St. William's from 1976 to 1990, is accused, along with the others, of abusing 19 former pupils. According to Prosecutor Richard Wright QC, Carragher harbored a "dedicated sexual attraction to children, particularly young boys," which he kept hidden "under a facade of respectability."

Cardoso, a 23-year-old former Portugal Under-21 international, has signed a three-year contract with Rangers after an unrevealed transfer fee was paid to Vitoria Setubal, where he played 23 times last season following a move from Benfica. In an interview with Rangers TV, Cardoso conveyed his excitement about adapting to his new life and expressed optimism about his future, pledging to help the team achieve success while acknowledging the high standards at Rangers. He is the second Portuguese center-back to join Rangers this summer, after Bruno Alves from Cagliari, and his arrival coincides with the loan signing of midfielder Dalcio from Benfica to Ibrox.

With the next election on the horizon, veteran Mugabe rival Morgan Tsvangirai and former Vice-President Joice Mujuru have declared an alliance, though they haven't yet chosen their presidential candidate. The 93-year-old incumbent, President Mugabe, who has governed Zimbabwe since its independence in 1980, plans to seek re-election. Tsvangirai hailed their collaboration as "the foundation for creating a wide-ranging coalition to challenge Zanu-PF." This union is vital for consolidating a divided opposition and, should it prove effective, would constitute the strongest unified opposition Mugabe has encountered since taking power in 1980.

Jean-Claude Juncker affirmed his backing for "democratic expressions" and vowed to honor Scotland's choice concerning its future during a Wednesday discussion with European Parliamentarians. Asked by Catalan MEP Josep Maria Terricabras about the possibility of Catalonia and Scotland joining the EU, Juncker responded that a mere membership application letter would not suffice. Later, in answer to a question from Scottish UKIP MEP David Coburn regarding an independent Scotland's EU standing, Juncker explained that the final determination lies with the United Kingdom.

An exposé revealed that a private Facebook chat among incoming Harvard students contained deeply offensive material, including jokes about child abuse, sexual assault, pedophilia, the Holocaust, and racism. Harvard's reaction, described as "draconian" by free speech proponents, was covered by the Crimson, the university's student newspaper. This chat, a spin-off from a broader messaging group for the incoming class, was designed for sharing memes and more mature content, with entry requiring the creation and sharing of a "provocative" meme. After the group's discovery, Harvard administrators launched an inquiry and interviewed the students involved.

In the wake of the controversial Brock Turner sentencing in June 2016, community leaders in Santa Clara County launched a petition drive on Monday to potentially recall Judge Aaron Persky in the next year. Persky, the judge in the case, sentenced Turner to six months in jail for sexual assault in January 2015, a much lighter sentence than the possible 14 years, and Turner was released after only three months. The recall effort references the global outrage over what was seen as Persky's overly lenient sentencing of Turner for assaulting an unconscious woman. Michele Dauber, a Stanford law professor leading the recall campaign with 50 other community leaders, stated at a press conference that residents of Santa Clara County deserve a judge who values victim safety more than the rights of rapists, highlighting the commitment of women to fighting rape culture through concrete action.

Each year, contestants vie for the top spot by creating and delivering the most inventive and convincing tall tale in under five minutes. This year's unexpected victor was George Kemp from Maryport, Cumbria, who overcame a chest infection to win with his story about "meeting Donald Trump and his wife at an underwater hotel." Kemp's narrative involved "building a small submarine out of his father's old bubble car." He elaborated, "We drove to the Isle of Man in the bubble car and met various celebrities on a Scottish submarine made from shortbread tins. Afterward, Nicola Sturgeon and Alex Salmond sold numerous large shortbread tin submarines to the United States." Mike Naylor, a.k.a. Monkey Liar, from Wasdale and last year's champion, took second place, and Helen Jordan finished third. Celebrated past winners include comedian and TV star Sue Perkins.

The inquiry found that 28% of Welsh speakers had used the language with their GPs, dentists, or opticians. Ms. Huws expressed her hope that the report would trigger significant change, leading to patient-centered healthcare. Government ministers received the report positively and promised a response within half a year. Based on the experiences of more than a thousand Welsh speakers, the study emphasized that 90% felt they should have the right to communicate in Welsh with the NHS, irrespective of where they lived in Wales. Furthermore, Welsh speakers reported feeling uneasy and struggling to communicate with doctors who were not fluent in Welsh. The report put forward 33 recommendations to the Welsh government, pressing ministers to offer explicit policy guidance, an implementation strategy, and a schedule for reforming primary healthcare.

The proposed law aims to revoke sections of the UK's 2016 Trade Union Act, potentially changing current restrictions on strikes in the NHS, fire services, schools, and other services managed by the Welsh government. UK government officials insist that industrial relations are a matter for Westminster, noting that the UK law requires strike action to be supported by 40% of a union's members via ballot. The Welsh Assembly's Equality, Local Government and Communities Committee agreed that the proposed legislation is vital for preserving Wales' collaborative "social-partnership" approach. Welsh Finance Secretary Mark Drakeford stated in March that it would be a "democratic outrage" if London tried to block the Welsh Trade Union Bill. The Labour-led Welsh Government argues that UK ministers should not limit union activities in Welsh devolved sectors like healthcare and education. Conservative AM Janet Finch-Saunders disagreed with the committee report, preventing its unanimous approval.

After the tragic death of 11-year-old Evha Jannath, who fell from a boat on the Splash Canyon ride at Drayton Manor during a school trip on Tuesday, other theme parks have responded. Drayton Manor will remain closed on Friday to carry out safety checks. Merlin Entertainments, which runs Alton Towers and Legoland Windsor, has temporarily shut down comparable water rides as a safety measure, with plans to reopen them on Friday. However, Lightwater Valley and West Midland Safari Park have decided to keep their water rides running following the incident.

Rangers secured the trophy after three previous failed attempts, thanks to Ally Gilchrist's own goal and a strong strike from James Tavernier that gave them a significant advantage. Andy Halliday's penalty and Kenny Miller's goal from close range further cemented Rangers' triumph. Mark Warburton's team is now preparing to face Celtic in the Scottish Cup semi-final next Sunday. Having overcome earlier Challenge Cup losses to Queen of the South, Raith Rovers, and Alloa Athletic, Rangers finally won the title and are now preparing to play the Premiership leaders at Hampden. Before the game, a new pitch will be installed to fix the current one's substandard condition. The existing pitch, which cost £200,000 and was installed just five weeks ago, will be replaced because of settling problems, making it unsafe for the final match between Rangers and League One's Peterhead, who were heavy underdogs at 22-1.

The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) is poised to hold its inaugural strike in its 134-year history, following an overwhelming 90% vote in support of the action. The Department of Health has voiced its regret over the planned strike, promising to work with trusts to ensure the safety of mothers and babies and reaffirming its commitment to ongoing dialogue. The RCM is urging immediate talks with the health minister to resolve the current deadlock. Bredagh Hughes, RCM NI director, explained that midwives are seeking pay parity with colleagues in Wales, Scotland, and England, who have already received a 1% pay increase. She clarified that the dispute lies with the Department of Health and employers, not the women in their care, and guaranteed that full emergency services would remain operational, ensuring women's safety, even if striking midwives are needed to fill staffing shortages.

Tesco Bank has revised its estimate of affected current account holders to under 10,000, significantly down from the initial 20,000, confirming no personal data compromise. The bank has fully reimbursed all impacted customers. CEO Benny Higgins characterized the weekend's events as "a systematic, sophisticated attack," emphasizing that affected customers were compensated and that the temporary block on online debit transactions was removed, returning accounts to normal. The restriction on online debit card payments, enacted Sunday to prevent further criminal activity, is now lifted. Higgins apologized again for the worry and inconvenience caused, underscoring the bank's grasp of the attack's nature.

A BBC London and Newsnight investigation revealed widespread fraud within the Construction Skills Certification Scheme (CSCS), the UK's leading certification program ensuring construction workers possess necessary skills and safety knowledge. The Construction Industry Training Board's (CITB) Carl Rhymer stated that 6,000 cardholders must now re-sit their tests. The CSCS card, mandated by nine major UK construction companies, Crossrail, and Heathrow, was undermined by corrupt test centers that assured passing scores for a fee. This allowed workers with poor English skills to gain certifications and work in dangerous construction environments. The BBC's probe centered on Wep HSE in Ealing, where director Garet Estensen was seen providing answers to candidates via a screen. Estensen refused to comment when confronted with the evidence. Future Training was also implicated as a participating center.

Hackers are demanding a ransom of 100 Bitcoin, equivalent to around $70,000, after infiltrating the city's transportation network. In response to the attack, employees disconnected all ticket vending machines. The cyberattack crippled computers across the Municipal Transportation Agency (Muni), including those in stations, displaying a message from the perpetrators demanding payment and providing a contact email address at Yandex, a Russian email and social media provider. The message stated: "You Hacked, ALL Data Encrypted. Contact For Key(cryptom27@yandex.com)ID:681 ,Enter”. Despite the disruption, train services continued to operate, and city officials have initiated a comprehensive investigation. A spokesperson assured the BBC that the incident had "no impact to the transit service, to our safety systems or to our customer's personal information,” and stated that further details were unavailable due to the ongoing investigation. Muni is responsible for managing the city's trains, streetcars, and buses.

In the madison's concluding race, Belgians Moreno de Pauw and Kenny de Ketele beat the British duo. Although 36-year-old Wiggins plans to retire after the Ghent Six Day race in November, he quipped that he might rethink his decision if offered enough money. Expressing his love for racing, he admitted the week's events made him doubt his retirement. The five-time Olympic champion considered the Lee Valley velodrome, where he developed as a cyclist and which hosted the London 2012 track events, an appropriate venue to end his British racing career, telling Eurosport it brought back "fantastic memories" and that he expects to return, probably as a spectator, next year. Wiggins and Cavendish started competing in the event last Tuesday.

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) report revealed that the aircraft responded to the pilot's commands, based on cockpit recordings. The report confirmed that pilot Andy Hill, 51, ejected from the plane during the August 22nd crash, but whether he triggered the ejection is still unknown. Hill remains hospitalized in serious but stable condition. The AAIB also reported that the Hawker Hunter's canopy detached upon initial impact, causing the release and ignition of fuel and vapor. The jet then broke into four parts, ejecting both Hill and his seat. The investigation continues to explore "whether the pilot tried to initiate ejection or if the impact damage to the cockpit caused the canopy and pilot's seat to be released."

Around 200 top-tier athletes and potentially 25,000 recreational runners are set to participate in the 13.1-mile half marathon on Saturday, March 26th. The race starts close to Cardiff Castle and finishes on King Edward VII Avenue, in the heart of the city. Dave Bedford, a former world record holder in the 10,000m, lauded the course for its level terrain and its blend of Cardiff's historical appeal with its contemporary progress. Runners will pass landmarks including the Millennium Stadium, Cardiff City Stadium, Penarth Marina, Cardiff Bay Barrage, Wales Millennium Centre, and Roath Park Lake, before a grand finale in the city center. This 2016 championship is the first time the event has been held in Wales. Cardiff, which has hosted a yearly half marathon since 2003, expects that hosting the World Half Marathon will solidify its reputation as a leading racing venue.

Falkirk Council is set to declare the area between Bo'ness Harbour and the former Kinneil colliery as its second Local Nature Reserve, creating a haven for local plants and animals. The council aims to use this designation to unlock funding for the area's preservation. This new status marks a transformation for the site, which was an industrial hub for almost 200 years until the main colliery shut down in 1983. Parts of the area were already recognized for their ecological importance, with the mudflats and offshore "island" designated as a Special Protection Area due to their conservation value. Councillor Adrian Mahoney, the spokesperson for leisure, tourism, and communities, welcomed the Kinneil foreshore's new status, pointing out that it marks 30 years since the closure of Kinneil Colliery, the last mine in the area.

Spencer Flower, a 72-year-old Conservative councillor representing Verwood, Dorset, has been found guilty of unlawful voting. The Bournemouth Magistrates' Court determined that Flower violated the Localism Act 2011 by failing to disclose his association with a social housing company during a 2013 discussion regarding an east Dorset housing project, from which the company stood to benefit if approved. Although convicted, Flower will remain in his council seat. He received a conditional discharge lasting six months and was ordered to pay Â£930 in costs. Upon leaving the court, Flower expressed "surprise and disappointment," characterizing the conviction as based on a "technicality." While refraining from commenting on his political future, he emphasized that the conditional discharge was the "lowest possible penalty" and that the court recognized the lack of proof showing "any personal gain or intent."

In 1964, Cilla Black, who died in 2015, achieved a UK top 10 hit with "It's for You," a song written by John Lennon and Paul McCartney. McCartney had originally recorded the song himself that year before giving it to Black after her performance at the London Palladium. The recording, which was thought to be lost, was found by Black's nephew. Frustrated by the intricate and lengthy automated menus of call centres, Mr. Clarke started this project. His investigation showed that some systems offer nearly 80 different options, potentially making callers wait for more than four minutes just to connect to the right department. He explained that even though reaching an HM Revenue and Customs advisor only needs four button presses, the whole process can take six minutes because of the time spent listening to each menu option. In reply, HMRC emphasized its dedication to better service, with a representative saying, "HMRC is exploring methods to enhance its interactive voice responses and intends to implement new speech recognition technology." This technology seeks to allow the system to comprehend spoken requests, removing the need for button presses. Mr. Clarke pointed out that HMRC expects to put these improvements into effect later this year.

Despite Syria's failure to meet the Sunday deadline for removing its chemical weapons, envoy Sigrid Kaag stressed the need to meet the June 30 target for complete destruction. The agreement between Russia and the US to eliminate Syria's chemical weapons was initiated due to a fatal sarin attack near Damascus the previous year. This international undertaking, supervised by the UN Security Council and the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), seeks to dismantle Syria's chemical weapons program. Even though past deadlines were missed, Damascus committed to removing its entire stockpile by April 27, while the overall UN deadline remains June 30. Kaag, head of the OPCW-UN mission, acknowledged the removal of a considerable amount of chemical weapons material, but highlighted the need for destruction, emphasizing the urgency of removing the remaining material from the last site to meet the final deadline.
